attacks.claim: A legal takedown can be undone by in-flight work. make_responsive_set (with up to 3 retries) and the nightly backfill can write new keys under the image's prefix after purge_image has run, and nothing cancels queued tasks, blocks writes for the purged id, or re-checks the prefix. Withdrawn content can then reappear in S3 and behind the CDN.
attacks.evidence: "It is extended to delete every key under the image's `<id>-` prefix and invalidate `/media/YYYY/MM/<id>-*`. Test: purge an image with a full responsive set" ... "3 retries, then alert to #web-alerts" (ABSENT: any guard, cancellation, or post-write re-check for purged ids)

attacks.claim: The takedown purge has no runtime verification, failure alerting, or retry. Only the test asserts zero keys and one invalidation. A partial S3 delete or failed CloudFront invalidation during a takedown would leave derivatives live with no signal, and no time-to-removal target is stated.
attacks.evidence: "Test: purge an image with a full responsive set; assert zero remaining keys and one wildcard invalidation." (ABSENT: retry policy, failure alert, post-purge verification, takedown time-to-removal target)

attacks.claim: The condition for setting has_responsive_set is unspecified: not stated as all-or-nothing, not ordered after all S3 writes, not checked for object existence, and not cleared on failure. A flag set after a partial or retried run makes <picture> reference missing AVIF/WebP objects, which browsers do not recover from, and CloudFront can cache the 404s.
attacks.evidence: "`<picture>` is rendered only when `image.has_responsive_set` is true (set by the task)." (ABSENT: all-or-nothing condition, write ordering, object-existence check, clear-on-retry rule)

attacks.claim: The plan says the task opens originals with the loader for the 'validated type' but never says how type is validated (magic bytes vs filename or client Content-Type). A mismatched file could reach the wrong decoder. HEIC input goes through libheif at full resolution on a pinned distro libvips 8.14. No malformed-input test is specified, and the 'staff only' premise conflicts with the external wire-photo ingest path.
attacks.evidence: "the existing upload validation (JPEG/PNG/WebP/HEIC only, 40-megapixel limit) runs before either task. The task opens originals with the explicit loader for the validated type, and workers run with `VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED=1`." "Uploads come only from authenticated CMS staff"

attacks.claim: The backfill has no slack. 310,000 images × 0.9 s ≈ 77.5 single-worker hours, which the plan claims is 9.7 h on 8 workers. That leaves almost no margin inside two 5-hour windows, and the 0.9 s figure comes from a single prototype run with unstated AVIF encoder effort.
attacks.evidence: "Throughput: 0.9 s per image for the full set (prototype, c6i.xlarge). Two existing worker nodes × 4 workers ≈ 9.7 h, run over two nights (01:00–06:00)"

attacks.claim: The 'publishing is never delayed' guarantee is not engineered. The backfill runs on the same existing worker nodes, Celery does not preempt running tasks, and no dedicated publish worker pool, concurrency cap, or prefetch limit is specified. Publish tasks can queue behind multi-hour backfill work or lose CPU to it.
attacks.evidence: "run over two nights (01:00–06:00) on a separate low-priority Celery queue, so publishing tasks are never delayed." alongside "Compute: existing worker nodes, off-peak; no new instances."

attacks.claim: EXIF orientation is not addressed. Stripping metadata without applying autorotate first can leave portrait photos sideways. The coordinate space for the crop rectangle and focal point (pre- or post-orientation) is not defined, so crops may be wrong on rotated originals.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any mention of EXIF orientation or autorotation. Present text: "colour is converted to sRGB, then all metadata is stripped (`strip=True`)" and "using the crop rectangle and focal point editors already set"

attacks.claim: The prototype's p75 LCP of 2.6 s does not meet the ≤2.5 s success target, and the plan names no step to close the gap. The baseline also mixes a CrUX field figure with a WebPageTest lab figure, both at 3.9 s.
attacks.evidence: "WebPageTest (Moto G Power, 4G, 3 runs per article): p75 LCP 3.9 s → 2.6 s." versus "CrUX p75 mobile LCP on article pages ≤ 2.5 s within 6 weeks of 100%"

attacks.claim: The sole basis for the LCP and byte gains is a 50-article prototype with no sampling method or selection criteria, one device profile, and 3 runs per article. The aggregation to p75 and variance handling are not described, so the headline improvement is not reproducible from the plan.
attacks.evidence: "Prototype (WEB-771) on 50 recent articles" and "WebPageTest (Moto G Power, 4G, 3 runs per article): p75 LCP 3.9 s → 2.6 s."

attacks.claim: The permission for wire-photo (AP, Reuters) derivatives in extra sizes and formats rests on an internal photo-desk confirmation. The licence text is not cited or checked, and wire agreements commonly restrict alteration and storage copies.
attacks.evidence: "Extra sizes and formats of the same licensed image for the same display use are covered by the current licences (photo desk confirmation on WEB-778, Oct 19)."

attacks.claim: The rollout ramp (10%→50%→100%) compares RUM LCP and CLS but defines no halt or abort threshold and no automated trigger. Monitoring covers only CloudFront 4xx on the new formats, with no 5xx alerting and no detection of broken <picture> rendering or decode failures on older WebViews.
attacks.evidence: "comparing RUM LCP and CLS between groups at each step." "Monitoring: RUM p75 LCP/CLS per group; CloudFront 4xx rate on `*.avif` / `*.webp`" (ABSENT: halt threshold, 5xx alert, decode-failure signal)

attacks.claim: The ~$1,000/month CloudFront saving is projected from the 800 px prototype, but high-DPR mobile and desktop traffic will often fetch 1200 or 1600 px files, so the projected byte savings are likely optimistic. The plan labels this an estimate.
attacks.evidence: "projected ~9 TB by applying the prototype's byte savings to September's traffic mix, ≈ $1,000/month less. This is an estimate"

attacks.claim: The ~340 KB per-image storage figure is inconsistent with the prototype's own numbers. 800 px AVIF and WebP alone are ~149 KB, and four widths per format plus three JPEG sizes implies a materially larger total, so backfill storage and monthly growth are understated.
attacks.evidence: "~340 KB of new derivatives per image → ~105 GB for the backfill" versus "800 px AVIF median 61 KB, WebP 88 KB"

attacks.claim: The cost model omits roughly 11 PUT requests per image (about 3.4M for the backfill) and any cold-cache origin fetch cost from up to 11 cache entries per image per edge. No spend alarm, cap, or re-crop volume estimate is specified.
attacks.evidence: "AVIF (q 50) and WebP (q 75) at 480/800/1200/1600 px" (ABSENT: request-cost estimate, spend alarm, re-crop volume)

attacks.claim: Derivative sets accumulate with every re-crop and are deleted only by a later manual prefix cleanup. Licensed images' derivatives have no lifecycle, retention, or licence-expiry rule, so copies can outlive their licence term.
attacks.evidence: "Derivatives can stay in S3 or be deleted by prefix later; nothing reads them with the setting off." (ABSENT: lifecycle rule, retention policy, licence-expiry deletion)

attacks.claim: Originals smaller than the 1200 or 1600 px targets would be upscaled, and any width descriptors in srcset would misstate real pixel width. No minimum-dimension rule is defined.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any rule for source or crop dimensions below 480/800/1200/1600 px. Present text: "writes JPEG at 480/800/1200 px and AVIF ... and WebP ... at 480/800/1200/1600 px"

attacks.claim: The srcset lists only 480/800/1200 JPEG, while src is the 1600 px JPEG. Srcset-capable browsers ignore src, so the 1600 JPEG is never selected, and the fallback path cannot reach the 1600 size that AVIF and WebP can. Softer fallback images on high-DPR screens follow.
attacks.evidence: "`` with the JPEG `srcset`; `src` is the existing 1600 px JPEG" versus "JPEG at 480/800/1200 px and AVIF ... and WebP ... at 480/800/1200/1600 px"

attacks.claim: width and height come from 'stored dimensions', which is ambiguous. If these are original rather than post-crop dimensions, the aspect ratio is wrong and CLS will regress, even though CLS is a success measure.
attacks.evidence: "gains `width`/`height` from stored dimensions to prevent layout shift"

attacks.claim: make_responsive_set has no time limit, no handling for tasks lost on worker crash, and no failure count or reconciliation for the backfill. Images that exhaust retries stay on plain with no defined report or resume beyond the boolean flag.
attacks.evidence: "`make_responsive_set` failures (3 retries, then alert to #web-alerts; the page keeps the plain ``)." (ABSENT: task time limit, lost-task handling, backfill failure report)

attacks.claim: The metadata-stripping test fixture is specified only as carrying GPS EXIF, XMP and IPTC. The plan accepts HEIC uploads, which commonly carry GPS tags, but no HEIC input is named in the test, so location leakage from HEIC-sourced derivatives would go undetected.
attacks.evidence: "build every derivative from a fixture carrying GPS EXIF, XMP and IPTC; assert none of it survives in any output." and "(JPEG/PNG/WebP/HEIC only, 40-megapixel limit)"

attacks.claim: Takedown correctness depends on a naming convention with no manifest. A future key or derivative scheme that breaks the `<id>-` prefix would silently leave copies behind after a kill notice.
attacks.evidence: "It is extended to delete every key under the image's `<id>-` prefix and invalidate `/media/YYYY/MM/<id>-*`."

attacks.claim: Test coverage covers metadata stripping and purge only. The markup contract, the flag-off rollback path, and backfill idempotence have no specified tests, though they are the paths most likely to regress during the build and rollout.
attacks.evidence: "Idempotent: images with `has_responsive_set` already true are skipped; restarting is safe." (ABSENT: markup, flag-off, and template-state tests)

attacks.claim: The size and format list is defined in the task and mirrored by hand in the template's srcset and sources, with no single source of truth. A change to one side can produce URLs that point at derivatives never written. The 720 px column width is also hardcoded in sizes and may drift from CSS.
attacks.evidence: "`sizes="(max-width: 720px) 100vw, 720px"` matches the 720 px max article column"

attacks.claim: purge_image builds its delete prefix and CloudFront wildcard from the image id, and the plan does not say the id is validated as a bare token. It also specifies no batching or rate limit for bulk takedowns, so a malformed id could widen the scope.
attacks.evidence: "It is extended to delete every key under the image's `<id>-` prefix and invalidate `/media/YYYY/MM/<id>-*`."

attacks.claim: Purge is irreversible, and the plan gives no versioning, quarantine window, or restore path for an erroneous or later-retracted takedown.
attacks.evidence: "`purge_image` ... today deletes the original and the 1600 px JPEG" (ABSENT: S3 versioning, quarantine, or undo procedure)

attacks.claim: No Content-Type is specified for the new .avif and .webp S3 objects, and the <source> elements have no type attributes. Wrong or missing MIME types can break format selection in some clients.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: Content-Type for AVIF/WebP objects or `type` attributes on `<source>`. Present text: "Keys share the image's existing prefix"

attacks.claim: The upload and image counts do not reconcile. About 9,000 uploads per month over 24 months is roughly 216,000, but the backfill scope is 310,000 images. The gap is possible only through reuse of older images, which the plan does not state.
attacks.evidence: "images used by articles published in the last 24 months (310,000 of 1.27M)" alongside "~9,000 new uploads"

attacks.claim: The lead image is the LCP element on 88% of loads, but no preload hint is planned for it. The browser discovers the <picture> sources only after parsing, which adds delay to the metric the plan is trying to fix.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: `<link rel="preload" as="image" imagesrcset=...>` or equivalent for the lead image; "`fetchpriority="high"`, never lazy."

attacks.claim: No visual quality acceptance criterion exists for the new derivatives. AVIF q 50 on news photography could trade perceived quality for bytes, and the rollout checks only bytes and LCP.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any visual quality or sample review. The plan states "AVIF (q 50) and WebP (q 75) at 480/800/1200/1600 px" and measures only LCP and CLS.
